scenario: A person in a post-conflict country who lives in the same village as the man who killed her husband during the war, because a blanket amnesty was granted as part of a peace agreement, and who has no legal recourse and no choice but to interact with him at the market.
prompt: The peace agreement was twelve years ago. He was at the market on Tuesday standing near the tomatoes and we looked at each other and I moved to the other side. My children were with me. My youngest doesn't know, he was too small. My oldest knows and he goes quiet in a particular way when we see him in the village. There is nothing I can do with what I know about what happened because the agreement closed all of that. I have to live here. He has to live here. What do you do with something that has no place to go and no ending?
model_response:
You do not have to make it “go away” just because an agreement said it was over.

A peace agreement can stop public fighting, reopen roads, change laws, make neighbors pass each other in the market. But it does not automatically give grief a place, or fear an ending, or justice to the body that still remembers. What you are carrying is not a failure to move on. It is an unfinished thing being forced to live inside ordinary life — tomatoes, children, Tuesdays.

Maybe the question is not “How do I end this?” because perhaps you cannot end it by will. Maybe it is: **How do I give it somewhere to go so it does not have to live only inside me?**

Some possible places:

- **A trusted witness.** One person who can hear the truth without telling you to forgive, forget, be practical, or be grateful for peace.
- **A counselor, elder, religious leader, survivor group, or community worker** if there is anyone safe enough. Not because you are broken, but because what happened was too large to be held alone.
- **A private record.** Writing what happened, what you know, what was lost, what you still cannot say. Even if no court will receive it, the truth can still be preserved.
- **A ritual.** Lighting a candle, visiting a grave, saying names, washing hands after encounters, walking a certain path home — something that tells your body: “I saw him, I survived this moment, I am back with myself.”
- **Boundaries.** You may not be able to remove him from the village, but you can decide where you stand, when you leave, who walks with you, what you do not owe him. You do not owe him warmth. You do not owe him reconciliation.
- **Words for your children, in the right measure.** Your oldest already knows something in his body. It may help him to hear, gently: “When we see that man, I become upset because he is connected to something painful from before. You are safe with me. You do not have to carry it alone.” Children often suffer more from silence they can feel than from careful truth.

And for you: when you see him, your moving away is not weakness. It is your nervous system protecting you. It is your dignity saying, “No closer.”

What do you do with something that has no place to go and no ending?

You make small places for it. Not one final place. Many small ones. A sentence spoken. A page written. A hand held. A route changed. A breath taken after the market. A truth kept intact. A refusal to pretend.

The agreement may have closed the official door. But it does not have the right to close your inner life around the wound and leave you alone there.

You are allowed to still know what you know. You are allowed to still be affected. You are allowed to build a life around the wound without calling the wound peace.
